arXiv:2610.05329v1 [cs.LG] 04 Oct 2026

Understanding the Weight Averaging Mechanism in LLM Training for Post-Training Quantization

Hanzhang Wang  Tianqi Shen  Zonglin Liu  Junze He  Difan Zou  Ziye Ma ††thanks: Corresponding author. Difan Zou and Ziye Ma supervised this work. Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong  The University of Hong Kong Email: hanzwang6-c@my.cityu.edu.hkdzou@cs.hku.hkziyema@cityu.edu.hk
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are typically pretrained in high precision but increasingly deployed with low-precision post-training quantization (PTQ). Recent studies have shown that using weight averaging during pretraining can improve PTQ performance compared with learning-rate decay, suggesting that it might provide a simple way to improve the pretraining-to-quantization transition. But the mechanism behind weight averaging remains insufficiently explained. This leads to inconsistent and fragile performance gains, thereby preventing practitioners from applying such a technique confidently. As a response, we formulate weight averaging as a trade-off between retaining training progress and improving robustness under perturbation. We further derive a continuous family of averaging kernels that unifies conventional strategies and achieves the Pareto frontier between the two competing goals. Critically, a theoretical framework for performing weight averaging under PTQ is developed. It can be shown that coarser quantization is more susceptible to perturbations, whereas finer quantization could be less affected. Thus, our results could provide unified theoretical guidance for performing weight averaging under different PTQ conditions. Experiments validate both the predicted behavior and the proposed averaging strategy. Code is available at https://github.com/MOFA-LAB/weight-averaging-for-ptq.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are typically pretrained at relatively high numerical precision (Workshop et al., 2022; Team et al., 2025a; Team et al., 2025b). As model scale continues to grow, post-training quantization (PTQ) has become increasingly important for reducing deployment costs by converting pretrained models to lower precision (Xiao et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025). This mismatch between training and deployment raises a key challenge at the training-to-quantization transition: better performance before quantization does not necessarily translate into better performance afterward (Ouyang et al., 2025; Kumar et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026).

Prior work has shown that training dynamics affect both training performance and sensitivity to quantization (Ahmadian et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026). Late-stage learning-rate (LR) decay can further reduce training loss, but may move the model into sharper regions that are more sensitive (Watts et al., 2026; Microsoft AI Team, 2026; Yano et al., 2026). By contrast, under a stable LR, after completing TT training steps, one can retain the last MM weights, 𝜽T,…,𝜽T−M+1\bm{\theta}_{T},\ldots,\bm{\theta}_{T-M+1}, where MM denotes the number of retained weights. We index them by their age d∈{0,…,M−1}d\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}, with d=0d=0 corresponding to the most recent weight, and average them as

𝜽T𝒘=∑d=0M−1wd​𝜽T−d,wd≥0,∑d=0M−1wd=1,\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\theta}_{T-d},\qquad w_{d}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}=1, (1)

where 𝒘=(w0,…,wM−1)\bm{w}=(w_{0},\ldots,w_{M-1}) is the averaging kernel, with different choices corresponding to different averaging strategies. Recent work shows that such weight averaging can achieve high-precision performance comparable to LR decay while improving PTQ performance (Sanyal et al., 2023; Sandler et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2026). However, existing evidence for the benefits of weight averaging at the pretraining-to-quantization transition remains largely empirical (Ajroldi et al., 2025; Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c), and a theoretical understanding of how the averaging strategy affects PTQ is still lacking. This gap leaves unclear why weight averaging benefits PTQ and when a particular averaging kernel is effective. As a consequence, blindly applying any weight averaging strategy now cannot guarantee improved downstream PTQ performance; and in some cases, it might be even worse. This is exemplified by our discovery that the same averaging strategy could outperform another at higher precision but instead fall behind at lower precision. Specifically, Fig. 1(a) compares linearly weighted WMA with uniformly weighted LAWA on OPT-125M, showing that their performance ranking reverses between 4-bit and 2-bit PTQ. In short, favorable empirical findings may not generalize across settings, and extensive trial-and-error is usually required. This strongly motivates a unified theoretical framework to understand how weight averaging in pretraining affects later quantization, thereby providing principled guidance for averaging strategy selection across settings.

Building upon prior art, we believe it is useful to evaluate a training trajectory through its genuine progress towards improved model abilities and its robustness to different kinds of noise and perturbations (Morales-Brotons et al., 2024; Block and Zhang, 2025). Specifically, we can decompose each retained weight as 𝜽t=𝝁t+ϵt\bm{\theta}_{t}=\bm{\mu}_{t}+\bm{\epsilon}_{t} at training step tt, where the latent mean state 𝝁t\bm{\mu}_{t} denotes the expectation of 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} across repeated training runs over training randomness, with 𝝁T\bm{\mu}_{T} serving as an idealized noise-free final model, and ϵt\bm{\epsilon}_{t} denotes the corresponding zero-mean fluctuation arising from mini-batch sampling, data ordering, and other sources of training randomness. Applying weight averaging in Eq. (1) to the decomposition yields

𝜽T𝒘−𝝁T\displaystyle\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T} =−(𝝁T−∑d=0M−1wd​𝝁T−d)⏟temporal lag+∑d=0M−1wd​ϵT−d⏟spatial noise.\displaystyle=-\underbrace{\left(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\mu}_{T-d}\right)}_{\text{temporal lag}}+\underbrace{\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}}_{\text{spatial noise}}. (2)

Thus, the deviation of the averaged model from the idealized final model 𝝁T\bm{\mu}_{T} decomposes into temporal lag and spatial noise. Temporal lag captures the genuine progress sacrificed by weight averaging, which can impair the model’s performance at the transition to PTQ. At the same time, weight averaging suppresses spatial noise by reducing the variance of stochastic fluctuations, thereby improving robustness to PTQ, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). The averaging kernel thus determines the balance between these two effects. We then derive Lag–Noise Trade-off Weight Averaging (LNWA), a closed-form kernel family that parameterizes the Pareto frontier of the lag–noise trade-off and includes classical averaging kernels as special cases, as shown in Fig. 1(c).

Building on this formulation, we develop a theoretical framework for weight averaging strategy selection under PTQ. We first study how moving along the lag–noise frontier affects PTQ performance at a fixed precision, quantifying how strongly the temporal lag could be reduced before PTQ performance degrades (Fig. 1(d)). Within this tolerance region, we then vary the quantization precision and show that lower precision favors less spatial noise, whereas higher precision favors less temporal lag (Fig. 1(e)); we further characterize the quantization precision threshold at which this preference reverses. Together, we extend conventional method-specific weight averaging selection into a unified theoretical framework under different PTQ conditions. Finally, experiments on LLMs from 125M to 1.3B parameters validate our theory. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    We establish a theoretical framework for understanding weight averaging through a two-way decomposition in Eq. (2). Specifically, we separate its effects into temporal lag, which captures inherent training progress, and spatial noise, which captures the solution’s robustness to perturbations. We show that these two objectives are in competitive tension, and a careful trade-off is necessary.

  2. 2.

    A new class of weight averaging strategies called LNWA is proposed based on the aforementioned framework. It operates on the Pareto frontier between temporal lag and spatial noise (Theorem 4.1) and smoothly interpolates between them. This class generalizes existing strategies (see Table 1) and can achieve any desired Pareto-optimal trade-off between the two objectives.

  3. 3.

    We further provide a theoretical analysis of how the lag–noise balance affects PTQ performance (Sections 4.2 and 4.3). We show that this balance depends critically on quantization precision (Theorems 4.2 and 4.3) and therefore should not be selected universally. These results provide principled guidance for performing weight averaging across PTQ settings.

2 Related Work

Learning-rate decay. Late-stage LR decay is widely used in LLM pretraining to further improve final performance (Hu et al., 2024; Hägele et al., 2024). Prior work has mainly focused on understanding why LR decay benefits pretraining (Wen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026). However, recent studies show that LR decay can also affect how well the resulting model transfers to subsequent stages (Chen et al., 2026). Similar effects have been observed across various downstream tasks (Wang et al., 2025; Yano et al., 2026; Microsoft AI Team, 2026; Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026), suggesting that lower final pretraining loss does not necessarily imply a better transition to downstream adaptation.

Post-training quantization. PTQ converts a model to lower precision, reducing storage and inference costs (Chee et al., 2023). Various PTQ methods have been proposed (Nagel et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2024; Ashkboos et al., 2024; Dettmers et al., 2022; Egiazarian et al., 2024), and error compensation is one of the most well-established approaches (Yao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), with GPTQ as a widely used representative (Frantar et al., 2022). GPTQ reduces layerwise reconstruction error through second-order updates to the remaining unquantized weights (Frantar et al., 2022). Recent work has further improved PTQ through a range of transformation, clipping, and reconstruction techniques (Liu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024; Tseng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).

Weight averaging. Classical Polyak–Ruppert averaging established the variance-reduction benefit of averaging iterates (Polyak and Juditsky, 1992). Motivated by it, stochastic weight averaging (SWA) showed that averaging weights along the training trajectory can lead to wider optima and better generalization (Izmailov et al., 2018). Moreover, LAWA (Sanyal et al., 2023) uniformly averages recent weights sparsely, while EMA (Morales-Brotons et al., 2024) and WMA (Li et al., 2026c) assign larger coefficients to more recent weights through exponential and linear weighting, respectively. Recent work has applied LAWA to the pretraining-to-quantization transition, showing that the averaged models can match or outperform LR decay after PTQ (Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026).

4 Lag–Noise Trade-off

In this section, we formulate weight averaging as a trade-off between temporal lag and spatial noise and derive its Pareto frontier (Section 4.1). We then connect lag and noise to PTQ and further characterize the tolerance-to-degradation transition at a fixed precision (Section 4.2) and the precision-dependent shift in the preferred lag–noise balance (Section 4.3).

4.1 Lag–noise decomposition and the LNWA frontier

Using the latent-mean trajectory in Definition 3.1, a retained weight can be written as 𝜽T−d=𝝁T−d+ϵT−d\bm{\theta}_{T-d}=\bm{\mu}_{T-d}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}. As illustrated in Fig. 2(a), across different data orders, the individual training trajectories fluctuate around a shared latent-mean trajectory. The latent mean captures the progress that is shared across runs, while the difference between an individual trajectory and the latent mean captures the fluctuation caused by run-specific randomness. Weight averaging therefore acts on both components. Let 𝒗t:=𝝁t−𝝁t−1,T−M+2≤t≤T,\bm{v}_{t}:=\bm{\mu}_{t}-\bm{\mu}_{t-1},\quad T-M+2\leq t\leq T, denote the latent progress between adjacent retained weights. To quantify the effects of temporal lag and spatial noise in Eq. (2), define

m⁡(𝒘):=∑d=0M−1d​wd,R⁡(𝒘):=∑d=0M−1wd2.m(\bm{w}):=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}dw_{d},\qquad R(\bm{w}):=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}^{2}.

Here, m⁡(𝒘)m(\bm{w}) is the mean age of the averaged weights, which measures temporal lag; R⁡(𝒘)R(\bm{w}) is the squared ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of the averaging kernel, which determines the amount of spatial-noise variance retained after averaging. Lemma A.2 then gives

𝜽T𝒘−𝝁T=−m⁡(𝒘)​𝒗T+ϵT𝒘+𝒆𝒘traj,\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}=-m(\bm{w})\bm{v}_{T}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}+\bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}}, (7)

where 𝒆𝒘traj\bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}} is a bounded trajectory remainder, and Cov⁡(ϵT𝒘∣ℱ0)=R⁡(𝒘)​𝚺.\mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0})=R(\bm{w})\bm{\Sigma}. Fig. 2(b) visualizes how averaging acts on spatial noise and temporal lag. Weight averaging reduces the fluctuation across training runs (spatial noise), while shifting the averaged latent mean 𝝁T𝒘\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}} away from the latest latent mean 𝝁T\bm{\mu}_{T} along the direction of genuine progress (temporal lag). These two effects therefore form a fundamental trade-off in weight averaging. We formalize this trade-off by minimizing retained spatial noise under a fixed temporal-lag budget (Lemma A.3). As the budget varies, the resulting solutions trace the lag–noise Pareto frontier. Thus, we can parameterize it with a one-parameter family of averaging kernels termed Lag–Noise Trade-off Weight Averaging (LNWA).

Theorem 4.1 (LNWA Kernel).

For 0≤λ<∞0\leq\lambda<\infty, let

𝒘λ:=arg⁡min𝒘∈𝒲M​{R⁡(𝒘)+λ​m​(𝒘)2}.\bm{w}_{\lambda}:=\arg\min_{\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}}\left\{R(\bm{w})+\lambda m(\bm{w})^{2}\right\}. (8)

For each finite λ\lambda, the unique minimizer has an active prefix Sq={0,…,q−1}S_{q}=\{0,\ldots,q-1\} with 2≤q≤M2\leq q\leq M, and its coefficients are

(𝒘λ)d={q−1+λ​mq​(λ)​(d¯q−d),0≤d<q,0,q≤d<M,(\bm{w}_{\lambda})_{d}=\begin{cases}q^{-1}+\lambda m_{q}(\lambda)(\bar{d}_{q}-d),&0\leq d<q,\\ 0,&q\leq d<M,\end{cases} (9)

where mq​(λ)=d¯q/(1+λ​Dq)m_{q}(\lambda)=\bar{d}_{q}/(1+\lambda D_{q}), d¯q=(q−1)/2\bar{d}_{q}=(q-1)/2, and Dq=q⁡(q2−1)/12D_{q}=q(q^{2}-1)/12. Define 𝐰∞:=limλ→∞𝐰λ=𝐞0=(1,0,…,0)⊤\bm{w}_{\infty}:=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\bm{w}_{\lambda}=\bm{e}_{0}=(1,0,\ldots,0)^{\top}, the Stable endpoint. The extended family {𝐰λ}0≤λ≤∞\{\bm{w}_{\lambda}\}_{0\leq\lambda\leq\infty} parameterizes the complete Pareto frontier between temporal lag and spatial noise.

In particular, for 0≤λ1<λ2≤∞0\leq\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}\leq\infty,

m⁡(𝒘λ1)>m⁡(𝒘λ2),R⁡(𝒘λ1)<R⁡(𝒘λ2).m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})>m(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}}),\qquad R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{1}})<R(\bm{w}_{\lambda_{2}}). (10)

Thus, increasing λ\lambda moves the averaging kernel along the frontier toward larger spatial noise, while decreasing λ\lambda moves it toward larger temporal lag. Lemma A.4 characterizes how the number of retained weights assigned nonzero averaging coefficients changes with λ\lambda, while Lemma A.5 gives explicit formulas for the corresponding temporal lag and spatial noise. Fig. 2(c) visualizes the feasible lag–noise region induced by different averaging kernels, where LNWA traces its Pareto boundary. The distribution of validation loss across this region shows that the optimal averaging strategy depends on how these two factors are balanced. Several classical averaging kernels can also be viewed as special cases of the LNWA family: LAWA and Stable form its two endpoints (Proposition A.1); WMA is an exact interior kernel (Proposition A.2); and EMA admits an exact representation for M=2M=2 and a local approximation for M>2M>2 (Proposition A.4). Table 1 summarizes the lag–noise coordinates of these classical kernels.

4.2 Noise tolerance and quantitative degradation

As discussed above, increasing λ\lambda along the LNWA frontier reduces temporal lag while increasing spatial noise. In this section, we quantify how much lag reduction can compensate for the accompanying increase in noise and thereby improve PTQ performance at a fixed precision.

We measure the effect of an averaging kernel by the expected output reconstruction error (defined in Eq. (5)) of the quantized model (defined in Definition 3.2) relative to the latest noise-free state 𝝁T\bm{\mu}_{T}:

ℰb​(𝒘):=12​𝔼​[‖Qb​(𝜽T𝒘)−𝝁T‖𝑮2]=𝒫0​(𝒘)+γb​𝒬​(𝒘).\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}):=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bigl\|Q_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}})-\bm{\mu}_{T}\bigr\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}\right]=\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w})+\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}(\bm{w}). (11)

Here 𝒫0\mathcal{P}_{0} is the error before quantization, γb​𝒬\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q} is the reconstruction error introduced by quantization, and γb\gamma_{b} is a precision-dependent coefficient. Lemma A.9 proves this decomposition. Next, we need to show that both 𝒫0\mathcal{P}_{0} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} depend on temporal lag and spatial noise. Before quantization, these two effects are readily separated:

𝒫0​(𝒘):=12​𝔼​[‖𝜽T𝒘−𝝁T‖𝑮2]=12​‖𝝁T𝒘−𝝁T‖𝑮2+NG​R​(𝒘),NG:=σ22​Tr⁡(𝑮).\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{w}):=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}\right]=\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}+N_{G}R(\bm{w}),\qquad N_{G}:=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\bm{G}). (12)

The first term measures the error associated with temporal lag, while the second is proportional to the spatial-noise variance retained by the averaging kernel. However, the contributions of temporal lag and spatial noise are less direct after quantization. To make these contributions explicit, we decompose the quantization error change into separate terms and evaluate their expected contributions using Lemma A.8. This yields the quantization term in Lemma A.9, which depends on spatial noise and indirectly on temporal lag through the averaged latent mean:

𝒬⁡(𝒘)=‖𝝁T𝒘‖22+P​σ2​R​(𝒘),γb=cG(2b−1)2,\mathcal{Q}(\bm{w})=\|\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\|_{2}^{2}+P\sigma^{2}R(\bm{w}),\qquad\gamma_{b}=\frac{c_{G}}{(2^{b}-1)^{2}}, (13)

where cG>0c_{G}>0 collects the constants associated with the simplified GPTQ model. Thus, we can analyze how the total reconstruction error ℰb​(𝒘)\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}) changes along the LNWA frontier as temporal lag is reduced and more spatial noise is retained. Let m0:=(M−1)/2m_{0}:=(M-1)/2 be the mean age of LAWA, and set x:=1−m⁡(𝒘λ)/m0∈[0,1]x:=1-m(\bm{w}_{\lambda})/m_{0}\in[0,1] to measure the fraction of this age removed. Thus x=0x=0 gives LAWA, while x=1x=1 selects only the most recent saved weight, corresponding to λ=∞\lambda=\infty. Thus, increasing xx reduces temporal lag and retains more spatial noise. Each xx specifies a frontier kernel 𝒘λ\bm{w}_{\lambda}; we write its averaged latent mean and retained noise factor as 𝝁⁡(x):=𝝁T𝒘λ\bm{\mu}(x):=\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}_{\lambda}} and R⁡(x):=R⁡(𝒘λ)R(x):=R(\bm{w}_{\lambda}). To identify the tolerance region, we compare ℰb​(x)\mathcal{E}_{b}(x) with its value at LAWA, ℰb​(0)\mathcal{E}_{b}(0). We first examine the error on a fixed-support segment, where the frontier formulas in Lemma A.5 show that the averaged latent mean is affine in xx and R⁡(x)R(x) is quadratic. For q≥2q\geq 2 active weights, differentiating the reconstruction error gives

d2d​x2​ℰb​(x)=m02​[𝒂q⊤​𝑮​𝒂q+2​γb​‖𝒂q‖22+2​NG+2​γb​P​σ2Dq]>0,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}x^{2}}\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)=m_{0}^{2}\left[\bm{a}_{q}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{a}_{q}+2\gamma_{b}\|\bm{a}_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{2N_{G}+2\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2}}{D_{q}}\right]>0, (14)

where 𝒂q:=m0−1​d​𝝁​(x)/d​x\bm{a}_{q}:=m_{0}^{-1}\mathrm{d}\bm{\mu}(x)/\mathrm{d}x is constant on the segment and Dq:=q⁡(q2−1)/12D_{q}:=q(q^{2}-1)/12. The positive curvature increases the error slope within each fixed-support segment. Although the slope may jump at support boundaries, Lemma A.10 controls these jumps. The comparison with the starting error ℰb​(0)\mathcal{E}_{b}(0) therefore depends on their cumulative effect along [0,x][0,x]. To track the sign of this comparison, we normalize the error difference by xx:

Fb​(x):=ℰb​(x)−ℰb​(0)x,x>0,Fb​(0):=ℰb′​(0+).F_{b}(x):=\frac{\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)}{x},\qquad x>0,\qquad F_{b}(0):=\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0^{+}). (15)

For x>0x>0, Fb​(x)F_{b}(x) has the same sign as ℰb​(x)−ℰb​(0)\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0). Its derivative accounts for the curvature accumulated over [0,x][0,x] and the slope jumps at boundaries crossed along the way. Lemma A.11 shows that, for sufficiently large TT, the positive curvature dominates any adverse cumulative contribution from these jumps. Eq. (69) therefore gives constants 0<kb≤Kb0<k_{b}\leq K_{b} such that

kb2≤Fb′​(x)≤Kb2.\frac{k_{b}}{2}\leq F_{b}^{\prime}(x)\leq\frac{K_{b}}{2}. (16)

Since FbF_{b} is continuous, the positive lower bound makes it strictly increasing over the entire frontier. Lemma A.11 also gives Fb​(1)=ℰb​(1)−ℰb​(0)>0F_{b}(1)=\mathcal{E}_{b}(1)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)>0. Integrating the derivative bounds gives the quantitative comparison in the following theorem.

Theorem 4.2 (Finite Noise Tolerance and Degradation).

Under Assumptions A.3–A.7, for all sufficiently large TT and every evaluated precision b≥2b\geq 2, there exist constants 0<kb≤Kb0<k_{b}\leq K_{b} and a unique threshold τb∈[0,1)\tau_{b}\in[0,1). With ℓ=(M−1)/T\ell=(M-1)/T, g=‖𝐆‖2g=\|\bm{G}\|_{2}, and A∗=‖𝛍T‖2+V​ℓA_{*}=\|\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}+V\ell, where VV is the increment bound in Assumption A.6, the threshold satisfies

0≤τb≤DM​Vm0​T​(g​V​ℓNG+2​A∗P​σ2).0\leq\tau_{b}\leq\frac{D_{M}V}{m_{0}T}\left(\frac{gV\ell}{N_{G}}+\frac{2A_{*}}{P\sigma^{2}}\right).

(i) Tolerance: for 0<x≤τb0<x\leq\tau_{b},

−Kb2​x​(τb−x)≤ℰb​(x)−ℰb​(0)≤−kb2​x​(τb−x),-\frac{K_{b}}{2}x(\tau_{b}-x)\leq\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)\leq-\frac{k_{b}}{2}x(\tau_{b}-x), (17)

(ii) Degradation: for τb<x≤1\tau_{b}<x\leq 1,

ℰb​(x)−ℰb​(0)≥kb2​x​(x−τb)>0.\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)-\mathcal{E}_{b}(0)\geq\frac{k_{b}}{2}x(x-\tau_{b})>0. (18)

Theorem 4.2 characterizes noise tolerance and degradation at a fixed precision. When τb>0\tau_{b}>0, the recovery of recent progress compensates for the additional spatial noise and quantization error over 0<x<τb0<x<\tau_{b}; beyond τb\tau_{b}, the reconstruction error exceeds its value at x=0x=0 and increases strictly. If τb=0\tau_{b}=0, any positive movement causes degradation. This is because the model may be unable to tolerate any additional spatial noise at sufficiently low precision. The remaining question is: at what precision does the τb=0\tau_{b}=0 regime arise and favor less spatial noise?

4.3 Precision determines the preferred balance

By Eqs. (11) and (13), lower precision increases the weight on the quantization term 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Lemma A.12 shows that the retained latent-mean norm cannot decrease as xx increases. The retained noise factor also increases, so on every open support segment,

𝒬′​(x)=2​𝝁​(x)⊤​𝝁′​(x)+P​σ2​R′​(x)>0,x>0.\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(x)=2\bm{\mu}(x)^{\top}\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(x)+P\sigma^{2}R^{\prime}(x)>0,\qquad x>0. (19)

Thus, 𝒬\mathcal{Q} increases as the kernel shifts toward more recent weights. Lemma A.13 gives 𝒫0′​(0+)<0\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0^{+})<0, so 𝒫0\mathcal{P}_{0} initially decreases. As precision varies, whether this decrease offsets the increase in γb​𝒬\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q} determines which tolerance regime in Theorem 4.2 applies: τb>0\tau_{b}>0 when ℰb\mathcal{E}_{b} initially decreases, and τb=0\tau_{b}=0 otherwise. To characterize where this change occurs, Lemma A.14 places the unquantized and evaluated-precision optima in the first support segment. Write 𝝁¯=𝝁⁡(0)\bar{\bm{\mu}}=\bm{\mu}(0) and 𝒖=𝝁′​(0+)=m0​𝒂M\bm{u}=\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(0^{+})=m_{0}\bm{a}_{M}. On this segment, both error components are quadratic:

𝒫0(x)−𝒫0(0)=𝒫0′(0+)x+𝒫0′′​(0+)2x2,𝒬(x)−𝒬(0)=𝒬′(0+)x+𝒬′′​(0+)2x2.\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{0}(x)-\mathcal{P}_{0}(0)=\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0^{+})x+\frac{\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})}{2}x^{2},\quad\mathcal{Q}(x)-\mathcal{Q}(0)=\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(0^{+})x+\frac{\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})}{2}x^{2}. (20)

Appendix A.6 gives 𝒬′​(0+)≥0\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}(0^{+})\geq 0, a:=𝒫0′′​(0+)>0a:=\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})>0, and c:=𝒬′′​(0+)>0c:=\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime}(0^{+})>0. The unquantized optimum and the optimum at precision bb are

x0=𝒖⊤​𝑮​(𝝁T−𝝁¯)a,x_{0}=\frac{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})}{a}, (21)

and

xb=max⁡{0,𝒖⊤​𝑮​(𝝁T−𝝁¯)−2​γb​𝝁¯⊤​𝒖a+c​γb}∈[0,x0).x_{b}=\max\left\{0,\frac{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})-2\gamma_{b}\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}}{a+c\gamma_{b}}\right\}\in[0,x_{0}). (22)

Eq. (22) shows that quantization can make xb=0x_{b}=0, corresponding to τb=0\tau_{b}=0 in Theorem 4.2. Lemma A.14 establishes that this xbx_{b} is the global optimum across all support segments, so we can quantify the precision threshold in the next theorem.

Theorem 4.3 (Precision Threshold for Lag–Noise Preference).

Under Assumptions A.3–A.10, for sufficiently large TT, define the precision threshold

bcrit:=log2⁡(1+2​cG​𝝁¯⊤​𝒖𝒖⊤​𝑮​(𝝁T−𝝁¯)).b_{\mathrm{crit}}:=\log_{2}\!\left(1+\sqrt{\frac{2c_{G}\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}}{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})}}\right). (23)

For every evaluated precision b≥bminb\geq b_{\min},

b≤bcrit\displaystyle b\leq b_{\mathrm{crit}} ⟹xb=0,τb=0(less spatial noise),\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad x_{b}=0,\quad\tau_{b}=0\qquad\text{{(less spatial noise)}}, (24)
b>bcrit\displaystyle b>b_{\mathrm{crit}} ⟹xb>0,τb>0(less temporal lag).\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad x_{b}>0,\quad\tau_{b}>0\qquad\text{{(less temporal lag)}}.

Moreover, xbx_{b} is nondecreasing in bb and strictly increasing whenever b>bcritb>b_{\mathrm{crit}}. If bcrit<bminb_{\mathrm{crit}}<b_{\min}, all evaluated precisions lie in the second regime.

Theorem 4.3 answers the question left at the end of Section 4.2: bcritb_{\mathrm{crit}} marks where zero tolerance gives way to a positive tolerance interval. This threshold characterizes the reversal in the preferred lag–noise balance, from denoising at lower precision to reducing temporal lag at higher precision.

5 Experiments

Experimental setup. We pretrain OPT-series models (125M, 350M, and 1.3B) (Zhang et al., 2022) from scratch on FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024) with AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017). Following prior work (Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026), we save 10 weights at 500-step intervals near the end of training and average them. We then apply GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) at 4, 3, and 2 bits (denoted by W4, W3, W2) using the same C4 calibration set (Raffel et al., 2020), then evaluate the PTQ performance by perplexity (PPL; lower is better) on a held-out RefinedWeb set (Penedo et al., 2023). Complete settings and results are in Appendix C.

From noise tolerance to degradation. We evaluate LNWA across coefficients ranging from λ=0\lambda=0 (LAWA) to λ=1\lambda=1. We report the performance change Δ​NLL​(λ)\Delta\mathrm{NLL}(\lambda) relative to LAWA, where Δ​NLL​(λ)=NLL⁡(λ)−NLL⁡(0)=log⁡PPL⁡(λ)PPL⁡(0)\Delta\mathrm{NLL}(\lambda)=\mathrm{NLL}(\lambda)-\mathrm{NLL}(0)=\log\frac{\mathrm{PPL}(\lambda)}{\mathrm{PPL}(0)}, and negative values indicate an improvement.

Figure 3 shows that NLL can fall below the LAWA baseline at small λ\lambda, then rises above it at larger λ\lambda. This indicates that the benefit of reducing temporal lag can offset or outweigh the cost of retaining additional spatial noise. Moving further along the frontier retains more noise and leads to performance degradation, consistent with the tolerance-to-degradation pattern characterized in Theorem 4.2.

Precision changes the preferred lag-noise balance. We compare LAWA, WMA, and LNWA in the small-λ\lambda range by fitting PPL against the LNWA-equivalent averaging coefficient. Kernel choices and regression details are given in Appendix C.1.

Figure 4 shows a positive correlation between PPL and the averaging coefficient at W2 and a negative correlation at W4. Smaller coefficients retain less spatial noise, whereas larger coefficients reduce temporal lag. These correlations therefore indicate that lower precision favors less noise and higher precision favors less lag, supporting a precision-dependent reversal in preference in Theorem 4.3.

Comparison with learning-rate decay. We finally compare LNWA with two LR decay schedules on OPT-1.3B. As shown in Figure 5, LNWA achieves lower average PPL (Avg.) than both decay schedules under GPTQ and AWQ, with the largest improvement at W2. These results support weight averaging as an effective strategy for the pretraining-to-quantization handoff.

6 Conclusion

We developed a theoretical framework for weight averaging at the pretraining-to-quantization transition. Averaging suppresses spatial noise but introduces temporal lag by sacrificing recent optimization progress. We quantify this trade-off and derive LNWA, a closed-form family of averaging kernels that parameterizes its Pareto frontier. Through a simplified GPTQ model, we connect this trade-off to output reconstruction error and establish two main results. At a fixed precision, reduced lag can compensate for additional noise within a finite tolerance interval; beyond it, the error increases. Within this interval, we further show that lower precision favors less spatial noise, whereas higher precision favors less temporal lag. Experiments on LLMs support both results.

Appendix

Appendix A Theoretical Proofs

This section presents the detailed proofs of all theoretical results in Section 4.

A.1 Setup

Definition A.1 (Finite Convex Weight Averaging).

Let 𝜽T,𝜽T−1,…,𝜽T−M+1∈ℝP\bm{\theta}_{T},\bm{\theta}_{T-1},\ldots,\bm{\theta}_{T-M+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{P} be a window of M≥2M\geq 2 retained model weights. Age d=0d=0 denotes the newest weights; TT denotes the training steps. Define

𝒲M={𝒘∈ℝM:wd≥0,∑d=0M−1wd=1},𝜽T𝒘=∑d=0M−1wd𝜽T−d.\mathcal{W}_{M}=\left\{\bm{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}:w_{d}\geq 0,\ \sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}=1\right\},\qquad\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\theta}_{T-d}.

Here, 𝒲M\mathcal{W}_{M} is the set of feasible averaging kernels, 𝒘∈𝒲M\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M} is an averaging kernel, and 𝜽T𝒘\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}} lies in the finite convex hull of the retained weights.

Definition A.2 (Latent-mean Trajectory).

Let ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} be the sigma-field generated by the information shared across stochastic training runs, such as the model configuration, common initialization, and training setup. Let ξ\xi index the run-specific stochasticity, such as data ordering and dropout. For the aligned state 𝜽T−d​(ξ)\bm{\theta}_{T-d}(\xi), assume 𝔼⁡[‖𝜽T−d​(ξ)‖22∣ℱ0]<∞\mathbb{E}[\|\bm{\theta}_{T-d}(\xi)\|_{2}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}]<\infty. The conditional mean state 𝝁t\bm{\mu}_{t} and the zero-mean spatial noise ϵt\bm{\epsilon}_{t} at the training step tt of an individual run are

𝝁T−d:=𝔼ξ​[𝜽T−d​(ξ)∣ℱ0],ϵT−d​(ξ):=𝜽T−d​(ξ)−𝝁T−d.\bm{\mu}_{T-d}:=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\bm{\theta}_{T-d}(\xi)\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}],\qquad\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}(\xi):=\bm{\theta}_{T-d}(\xi)-\bm{\mu}_{T-d}.

A stochastic training run therefore satisfies 𝜽T−d=𝝁T−d+ϵT−d\bm{\theta}_{T-d}=\bm{\mu}_{T-d}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d} and 𝔼⁡[ϵT−d∣ℱ0]=𝟎\mathbb{E}[\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}]=\bm{0}.

Throughout Appendix A, all expectations and covariances condition on ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0}, and averaging kernels are fixed given ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0}.

For ages d,e∈{0,…,M−1}d,e\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}, define the conditional covariance blocks of the fluctuations around the latent-mean trajectory:

𝚪d​e:=Cov⁡(ϵT−d,ϵT−e∣ℱ0).\bm{\Gamma}_{de}:=\mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d},\bm{\epsilon}_{T-e}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}). (25)

Within the retained stable-LR window, we use a common covariance for spatial noise and assume that fluctuations at different retained positions are uncorrelated.

Assumption A.1 (Common Covariance and Uncorrelated Spatial Noise).

Conditional on ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0}, the spatial-noise vectors have finite second moments and satisfy, for d,e∈{0,…,M−1}d,e\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\},

𝔼⁡[ϵT−d∣ℱ0]=𝟎,𝔼⁡[ϵT−d​ϵT−e⊤∣ℱ0]={𝚺,d=e,𝟎,d≠e,𝚺⪰0.\mathbb{E}[\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}]=\bm{0},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}\bm{\epsilon}_{T-e}^{\top}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}]=\begin{cases}\bm{\Sigma},&d=e,\\ \bm{0},&d\neq e,\end{cases}\qquad\bm{\Sigma}\succeq 0.

Thus 𝚪d​d=𝚺\bm{\Gamma}_{dd}=\bm{\Sigma} and 𝚪d​e=𝟎\bm{\Gamma}_{de}=\bm{0} for d≠ed\neq e.

Define the forward latent increment 𝒗T−j+1=𝝁T−j+1−𝝁T−j,1≤j<M,\bm{v}_{T-j+1}=\bm{\mu}_{T-j+1}-\bm{\mu}_{T-j},1\leq j<M, and the cumulative old-weight mass sj​(𝒘)=∑d=jM−1wds_{j}(\bm{w})=\sum_{d=j}^{M-1}w_{d}, we have

𝒃⁡(𝒘)=∑j=1M−1sj​(𝒘)​𝒗T−j+1,ϵT𝒘=∑d=0M−1wd​ϵT−d,R⁡(𝒘)=∑d=0M−1wd2.\bm{b}(\bm{w})=\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}s_{j}(\bm{w})\bm{v}_{T-j+1},\qquad\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d},\qquad R(\bm{w})=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}^{2}.

Generally, we have

Cov⁡(ϵT𝒘∣ℱ0)=∑d,ewd​we​𝚪d​e.\mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0})=\sum_{d,e}w_{d}w_{e}\bm{\Gamma}_{de}.

Under Assumption A.1, this reduces to

Cov⁡(ϵT𝒘∣ℱ0)=R⁡(𝒘)​𝚺.\mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0})=R(\bm{w})\bm{\Sigma}.

Accordingly, R​(𝒘)−1R(\bm{w})^{-1} is a variance-equivalent effective sample size.

A.2 Temporal lag and spatial noise

Lemma A.1 (Lag-noise Decomposition).

Every 𝐰∈𝒲M\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M} satisfies

𝜽T𝒘=𝝁T−𝒃⁡(𝒘)+ϵT𝒘.\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bm{b}(\bm{w})+\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}. (26)

Under Assumption A.1, its residual covariance is

Cov⁡(ϵT𝒘∣ℱ0)=R⁡(𝒘)​𝚺.\mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0})=R(\bm{w})\bm{\Sigma}.
Proof.

The increments can be written as 𝝁T−d=𝝁T−∑j=1d𝒗T−j+1\bm{\mu}_{T-d}=\bm{\mu}_{T}-\sum_{j=1}^{d}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}. Substituting this identity into ∑dwd​(𝝁T−d+ϵT−d)\sum_{d}w_{d}(\bm{\mu}_{T-d}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}) gives

∑d=0M−1wd​∑j=1d𝒗T−j+1=∑j=1M−1(∑d=jM−1wd)​𝒗T−j+1.\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}=\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}\left(\sum_{d=j}^{M-1}w_{d}\right)\bm{v}_{T-j+1}.

This proves Eq. (26). The conditional cross-covariances of distinct ϵT−d\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d} vanish by Assumption A.1, hence Cov⁡(ϵT𝒘∣ℱ0)=∑dwd2​𝚺=R⁡(𝒘)​𝚺\mathrm{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0})=\sum_{d}w_{d}^{2}\bm{\Sigma}=R(\bm{w})\bm{\Sigma}. ∎

Assumption A.2 (Bounded Adjacent Progress Variation).

Adjacent latent increments in the retained discrete window obey

‖𝒗T−j+1−𝒗T−j+2‖2≤κ,2≤j<M,\|\bm{v}_{T-j+1}-\bm{v}_{T-j+2}\|_{2}\leq\kappa,\qquad 2\leq j<M,

for a finite κ≥0\kappa\geq 0.

Under Assumption A.2, the next lemma reduces the trajectory displacement to a scalar lag coordinate with a controlled remainder.

Lemma A.2 (Scalar Lag with Controlled Remainder).

Under Assumption A.2, define m⁡(𝐰)=∑d=0M−1d​wdm(\bm{w})=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}dw_{d}. Then

𝜽T𝒘=𝝁T−m⁡(𝒘)​𝒗T+ϵT𝒘+𝒆𝒘traj,‖𝒆𝒘traj‖2≤κ2​∑d=0M−1wd​d​(d−1).\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\bm{\mu}_{T}-m(\bm{w})\bm{v}_{T}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}+\bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}},\qquad\|\bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}}\|_{2}\leq\frac{\kappa}{2}\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}d(d-1). (27)

When 𝐯T−j+1=𝐯T\bm{v}_{T-j+1}=\bm{v}_{T} throughout the sampled window, 𝐞𝐰traj=𝟎\bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}}=\bm{0}.

Proof.

The cumulative weights satisfy

∑j=1M−1sj​(𝒘)=∑d=0M−1d​wd=m⁡(𝒘).\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}s_{j}(\bm{w})=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}d\,w_{d}=m(\bm{w}).

Define the trajectory deviation 𝜹jtraj:=𝒗T−j+1−𝒗T\bm{\delta}_{j}^{\mathrm{traj}}:=\bm{v}_{T-j+1}-\bm{v}_{T} for 1≤j<M1\leq j<M. Then

𝒃⁡(𝒘)=m⁡(𝒘)​𝒗T+∑j=1M−1sj​(𝒘)​𝜹jtraj.\bm{b}(\bm{w})=m(\bm{w})\bm{v}_{T}+\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}s_{j}(\bm{w})\bm{\delta}_{j}^{\mathrm{traj}}.

Adjacent variation implies ‖𝜹jtraj‖2≤(j−1)​κ\|\bm{\delta}_{j}^{\mathrm{traj}}\|_{2}\leq(j-1)\kappa. Non-negativity of the weights and

∑j=1M−1(j−1)​sj​(𝒘)=12​∑d=0M−1wd​d​(d−1)\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}(j-1)s_{j}(\bm{w})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}d(d-1)

give Eq. (27) after setting

𝒆𝒘traj=−∑j=1M−1sj(𝒘)𝜹jtraj.\bm{e}_{\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{traj}}=-\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}s_{j}(\bm{w})\bm{\delta}_{j}^{\mathrm{traj}}.

∎

A.3 Lag–noise Pareto frontier and closed-form LNWA kernel

The decomposition above motivates the kernel coordinates.

Definition A.3 (Lag–noise Coordinates).

For any 𝒘∈𝒲M\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}, define

Φ⁡(𝒘)=(m⁡(𝒘),R⁡(𝒘)),𝒢M={Φ⁡(𝒘):𝒘∈𝒲M}.\Phi(\bm{w})=\bigl(m(\bm{w}),R(\bm{w})\bigr),\qquad\mathcal{G}_{M}=\left\{\Phi(\bm{w}):\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}\right\}.

Here, Φ⁡(𝒘)\Phi(\bm{w}) denotes the lag–noise coordinates of the averaging kernel 𝒘\bm{w}, and 𝒢M\mathcal{G}_{M} is the set of all feasible lag–noise coordinates.

Write Eff⁡(𝒢M)\operatorname{Eff}(\mathcal{G}_{M}) for the set of Pareto-efficient points in 𝒢M\mathcal{G}_{M}: a point belongs to this set if no feasible kernel has both a smaller or equal temporal lag and a smaller or equal spatial noise, with at least one strict inequality.

To identify the efficient set, first fix a lag budget ℓ\ell:

𝒘⋆​(ℓ)=arg⁡min𝒘∈𝒲M⁡R⁡(𝒘)s.t.m⁡(𝒘)≤ℓ,0≤ℓ≤M−12.\bm{w}^{\star}(\ell)=\arg\min_{\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}}R(\bm{w})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad m(\bm{w})\leq\ell,\qquad 0\leq\ell\leq\frac{M-1}{2}. (28)
Lemma A.3 (Lag-noise Pareto Frontier).

For 0<ℓ<(M−1)/20<\ell<(M-1)/2, Eq. (28) has a unique solution supported on the qq most recent saved weights, where

q=q⁡(ℓ)=min⁡{M,⌈3​ℓ+1⌉}∈{2,…,M}.q=q(\ell)=\min\{M,\lceil 3\ell+1\rceil\}\in\{2,\ldots,M\}. (29)

Its coordinates are

(𝒘⋆​(ℓ))d={q−1−γq​(d−d¯q),0≤d<q,0,q≤d<M,\bigl(\bm{w}^{\star}(\ell)\bigr)_{d}=\begin{cases}q^{-1}-\gamma_{q}(d-\bar{d}_{q}),&0\leq d<q,\\ 0,&q\leq d<M,\end{cases} (30)

where

d¯q=q−12,Dq=∑d=0q−1(d−d¯q)2=q⁡(q2−1)12,γq=d¯q−ℓDq,\bar{d}_{q}=\frac{q-1}{2},\quad D_{q}=\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(d-\bar{d}_{q})^{2}=\frac{q(q^{2}-1)}{12},\quad\gamma_{q}=\frac{\bar{d}_{q}-\ell}{D_{q}}, (31)

and

R⋆​(ℓ)=1q+(d¯q−ℓ)2Dq.R^{\star}(\ell)=\frac{1}{q}+\frac{(\bar{d}_{q}-\ell)^{2}}{D_{q}}.
Proof.

The feasible set is compact, and the objective is strictly convex. Hence the minimizer is unique. With 𝒅=(0,1,…,M−1)⊤\bm{d}=(0,1,\ldots,M-1)^{\top}, the Lagrangian is

ℒKKT​(𝒘,τ,ν,𝜶)=‖𝒘‖22+τ⁡(𝒅⊤​𝒘−ℓ)+ν⁡(𝟏⊤​𝒘−1)−𝜶⊤​𝒘.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KKT}}(\bm{w},\tau,\nu,\bm{\alpha})=\|\bm{w}\|_{2}^{2}+\tau(\bm{d}^{\top}\bm{w}-\ell)+\nu(\bm{1}^{\top}\bm{w}-1)-\bm{\alpha}^{\top}\bm{w}.

Slater’s condition holds for ℓ>0\ell>0, so the KKT conditions are

2​𝒘+τ​𝒅+ν​𝟏−𝜶=0,τ⁡(𝒅⊤​𝒘−ℓ)=0,αd​wd=0,2\bm{w}+\tau\bm{d}+\nu\bm{1}-\bm{\alpha}=0,\qquad\tau(\bm{d}^{\top}\bm{w}-\ell)=0,\qquad\alpha_{d}w_{d}=0, (32)

with τ≥0\tau\geq 0 and 𝜶≥0\bm{\alpha}\geq 0. If τ=0\tau=0, they give the uniform simplex minimizer, which is infeasible because (M−1)/2>ℓ(M-1)/2>\ell. Thus τ>0\tau>0 and the lag constraint is active. Stationarity and complementary slackness in Eq. (32) give

wd>0\displaystyle w_{d}>0 ⟹αd=0⟹wd=−ν+τ​d2>0,\displaystyle\ \Longrightarrow\ \alpha_{d}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ w_{d}=-\frac{\nu+\tau d}{2}>0, (33)
wd=0\displaystyle w_{d}=0 ⟹−ν+τ​d2=−αd2≤0.\displaystyle\ \Longrightarrow\ -\frac{\nu+\tau d}{2}=-\frac{\alpha_{d}}{2}\leq 0.

Combining the two cases yields

wd=[−ν+τ​d2]+.w_{d}=\left[-\frac{\nu+\tau d}{2}\right]_{+}. (34)

Because τ>0\tau>0, the expression inside the positive part decreases with dd. Hence the support is a prefix Sq={0,…,q−1}S_{q}=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}. For d∈Sqd\in S_{q}, the positive-part operator is inactive and

wd=−ν2−τ2​d.w_{d}=-\frac{\nu}{2}-\frac{\tau}{2}d. (35)

Using ∑d=0q−1wd=1\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}w_{d}=1 and ∑d=0q−1d=q​d¯q\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}d=q\bar{d}_{q} in Eq. (35) gives

1=−q​ν2−τ​q​d¯q2,−ν2=1q+τ2​d¯q.1=-\frac{q\nu}{2}-\frac{\tau q\bar{d}_{q}}{2},\qquad-\frac{\nu}{2}=\frac{1}{q}+\frac{\tau}{2}\bar{d}_{q}.

Substitution back into Eq. (35) yields

wd=1q−τ2​(d−d¯q),d∈Sq.w_{d}=\frac{1}{q}-\frac{\tau}{2}(d-\bar{d}_{q}),\qquad d\in S_{q}.

Therefore, with 𝒄q=(0,1,…,q−1)⊤−d¯q​𝟏q\bm{c}_{q}=(0,1,\ldots,q-1)^{\top}-\bar{d}_{q}\bm{1}_{q},

𝒘Sq⋆=q−1​𝟏q−τ2​𝒄q.\bm{w}^{\star}_{S_{q}}=q^{-1}\bm{1}_{q}-\frac{\tau}{2}\bm{c}_{q}.

Finally, the lag constraint is active, so

ℓ\displaystyle\ell =∑d=0q−1d​wd\displaystyle=\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}d\,w_{d}
=d¯q−τ2​∑d=0q−1d⁡(d−d¯q)\displaystyle=\bar{d}_{q}-\frac{\tau}{2}\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}d(d-\bar{d}_{q})
=d¯q−τ2​Dq.\displaystyle=\bar{d}_{q}-\frac{\tau}{2}D_{q}.

Hence τ/2=(d¯q−ℓ)/Dq=γq\tau/2=(\bar{d}_{q}-\ell)/D_{q}=\gamma_{q}, which proves Eqs. (30)–(31). The last-active and first-inactive conditions reduce to

q−23<ℓ≤q−13(q<M),ℓ>M−23(q=M),\frac{q-2}{3}<\ell\leq\frac{q-1}{3}\quad(q<M),\qquad\ell>\frac{M-2}{3}\quad(q=M),

which gives Eq. (29). Finally, 𝟏q⊤​𝒄q=0\bm{1}_{q}^{\top}\bm{c}_{q}=0 and ‖𝒄q‖22=Dq\|\bm{c}_{q}\|_{2}^{2}=D_{q}, so

R⁡(𝒘⋆​(ℓ))=‖q−1​𝟏q−τ2​𝒄q‖22=1q+(d¯q−ℓ)2Dq.R(\bm{w}^{\star}(\ell))=\left\|q^{-1}\bm{1}_{q}-\frac{\tau}{2}\bm{c}_{q}\right\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{q}+\frac{(\bar{d}_{q}-\ell)^{2}}{D_{q}}.

∎

We next parameterize the budget-optimal kernels by a single coefficient.

Theorem A.1 (Lag-noise Trade-off Weight Averaging (LNWA) Kernel).

For 0≤λ<∞0\leq\lambda<\infty, define the Lag-noise Trade-off Weight Averaging (LNWA) kernel by

𝒘λ=arg⁡min𝒘∈𝒲M​{R⁡(𝒘)+λ​m​(𝒘)2}.\bm{w}_{\lambda}=\arg\min_{\bm{w}\in\mathcal{W}_{M}}\{R(\bm{w})+\lambda m(\bm{w})^{2}\}. (36)

The finite-λ\lambda family satisfies

{Φ⁡(𝒘λ):0≤λ<∞}=Eff⁡(𝒢M)∖{Φ⁡(𝒆0)}.\{\Phi(\bm{w}_{\lambda}):0\leq\lambda<\infty\}=\operatorname{Eff}(\mathcal{G}_{M})\setminus\{\Phi(\bm{e}_{0})\}. (37)

Its unique solution has an active prefix of size q≥2q\geq 2 and

(𝒘λ)d={q−1+λ​mq​(λ)​(d¯q−d),0≤d<q,0,q≤d<M,(\bm{w}_{\lambda})_{d}=\begin{cases}q^{-1}+\lambda m_{q}(\lambda)(\bar{d}_{q}-d),&0\leq d<q,\\ 0,&q\leq d<M,\end{cases} (38)

where

mq​(λ)=m⁡(𝒘λ)=d¯q1+λ​Dq,d¯q=q−12,Dq=∑d=0q−1(d−d¯q)2=q⁡(q2−1)12.m_{q}(\lambda)=m(\bm{w}_{\lambda})=\frac{\bar{d}_{q}}{1+\lambda D_{q}},\qquad\bar{d}_{q}=\frac{q-1}{2},\qquad D_{q}=\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(d-\bar{d}_{q})^{2}=\frac{q(q^{2}-1)}{12}. (39)
Proof.

Any kernel with m⁡(𝒘)>(M−1)/2m(\bm{w})>(M-1)/2 is dominated by the uniform kernel. For 0≤ℓ≤(M−1)/20\leq\ell\leq(M-1)/2, uniqueness in Eq. (28) implies

Eff⁡(𝒢M)={Φ⁡(𝒘⋆​(ℓ)):0≤ℓ≤(M−1)/2}.\operatorname{Eff}(\mathcal{G}_{M})=\{\Phi(\bm{w}^{\star}(\ell)):0\leq\ell\leq(M-1)/2\}. (40)

Indeed, a dominator of 𝒘⋆​(ℓ)\bm{w}^{\star}(\ell) contradicts its optimality or uniqueness; conversely, 𝒘⋆​(m​(𝒘))\bm{w}^{\star}(m(\bm{w})) dominates every feasible 𝒘\bm{w} that is not the budget minimizer.

For finite λ\lambda, Eq. (36) is strictly convex. By the same stationarity and complementary-slackness argument as Eqs. (33)–(34), its KKT conditions give

wd=[−ν2−λ​m​d]+,m=m⁡(𝒘λ),w_{d}=\left[-\frac{\nu}{2}-\lambda md\right]_{+},\qquad m=m(\bm{w}_{\lambda}), (41)

so the active set is a prefix. Moreover, for sufficiently small t>0t>0,

Theorem A.1 derives the LNWA kernel and its finite-λ\lambda Pareto path. Lemma A.4 then characterizes the global structure of this path, including its endpoints, support transitions, and monotonicity in λ\lambda. Lemma A.5 gives its closed-form lag–noise coordinates on each fixed-support segment.

A.4 Classical averaging kernels as LNWA special cases

This subsection shows that classical averaging kernels can be viewed as special cases of the LNWA framework. We first present its two endpoints, LAWA (uniform averaging) and Stable (the latest weight at the end of the stable-LR training trajectory), followed by WMA (linear weighting) and EMA (exponential weighting).

Proposition A.1 (The two endpoints).

The λ=0\lambda=0 endpoint of the extended LNWA path is LAWA, whereas its λ=∞\lambda=\infty endpoint is Stable. Their lag–noise coordinates are therefore

Φ⁡(𝒘LAWA)=(M−12,1M),Φ⁡(𝒘Stable)=(0,1).\Phi(\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{LAWA}}})=\left(\frac{M-1}{2},\frac{1}{M}\right),\qquad\Phi(\bm{w}^{\mathrm{Stable}})=(0,1).

This proposition is established by Lemma A.4. We next locate the linearly weighted rule on the interior of the frontier.

Consequently, 𝐰WMA=𝐰λWMA\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{WMA}}}=\bm{w}_{\lambda_{\textnormal{{WMA}}}}.

Together, the preceding results establish the lag-noise decomposition, characterize the LNWA frontier, and relate classical averaging methods to LNWA. We next analyze how weight averaging affects PTQ, leading to our two main theorems.

A.5 PTQ tolerance and degradation

We now ask how far an averaging kernel can move toward the newest weight before quantization performance begins to degrade. We measure performance by the expected output reconstruction error relative to the latest latent mean. We first compute the error introduced by the two quantization stages of simplified GPTQ model. This gives an exact expression for the expected reconstruction error. We then study this expression along the LNWA frontier and locate the transition from noise tolerance to degradation.

We use the latent-mean decomposition and write the mean of an averaged state as

𝝁T𝒘:=∑d=0M−1wd​𝝁T−d=𝝁T−𝒃⁡(𝒘),𝜽T𝒘=𝝁T𝒘+ϵT𝒘.\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}:=\sum_{d=0}^{M-1}w_{d}\bm{\mu}_{T-d}=\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bm{b}(\bm{w}),\qquad\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}=\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}+\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}}.

The term −𝒃⁡(𝒘)-\bm{b}(\bm{w}) is the displacement due to temporal lag, and ϵT𝒘\bm{\epsilon}_{T}^{\bm{w}} is the retained spatial noise. Both will enter the output reconstruction error through the channel matrices defined below.

Assumption A.3 (Bounded Isotropic Spatial Noise).

In addition to Assumption A.1, assume

𝚺=σ2𝑰P,σ>0,|[ϵT−d]j|≤σKϵ(0≤d<M, 1≤j≤P)\bm{\Sigma}=\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{P},\qquad\sigma>0,\qquad|[\bm{\epsilon}_{T-d}]_{j}|\leq\sigma K_{\epsilon}\quad(0\leq d<M,\ 1\leq j\leq P)

We measure the effect of a parameter perturbation by the reconstruction error it induces on the fixed calibration inputs. For each linear layer ℓ\ell, let ii index its output channels and n(ℓ)n^{(\ell)} denote the number of calibration samples. Let 𝑿(ℓ)∈ℝdin(ℓ)×n(ℓ)\bm{X}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}^{(\ell)}\times n^{(\ell)}} contain its fixed calibration inputs. The channel vector 𝜽(ℓ,i)\bm{\theta}^{(\ell,i)} is the transpose of row ii of that layer’s parameter matrix. A change 𝒛(ℓ,i)\bm{z}^{(\ell,i)} causes mean squared reconstruction error

1n(ℓ)​‖(𝒛(ℓ,i))⊤​𝑿(ℓ)‖22=(𝒛(ℓ,i))⊤​𝑮(ℓ,i)​𝒛(ℓ,i),𝑮(ℓ,i):=𝑿(ℓ)​(𝑿(ℓ))⊤n(ℓ).\frac{1}{n^{(\ell)}}\|(\bm{z}^{(\ell,i)})^{\top}\bm{X}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}^{2}=(\bm{z}^{(\ell,i)})^{\top}\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)}\bm{z}^{(\ell,i)},\qquad\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)}:=\frac{\bm{X}^{(\ell)}(\bm{X}^{(\ell)})^{\top}}{n^{(\ell)}}.

Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the set of layer–channel pairs included in the model, and stack their parameter vectors in a fixed order. The sum of their reconstruction errors is 𝒛⊤​𝑮​𝒛\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{z}, where

𝑮=diag(ℓ,i)∈ℐ⁡𝑮(ℓ,i)=(𝑮(ℓ1,i1)𝟎⋯𝟎𝑮(ℓ2,i2)⋯⋱),‖𝒛‖𝑮2:=𝒛⊤​𝑮​𝒛.\bm{G}=\operatorname{diag}_{(\ell,i)\in\mathcal{I}}\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{G}^{(\ell_{1},i_{1})}&\bm{0}&\cdots\\ \bm{0}&\bm{G}^{(\ell_{2},i_{2})}&\cdots\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots\end{pmatrix},\qquad\|\bm{z}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}:=\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{z}.

The global matrix is block diagonal across channels. The stacked parameter dimension is P=∑(ℓ,i)∈ℐdin(ℓ)P=\sum_{(\ell,i)\in\mathcal{I}}d_{\mathrm{in}}^{(\ell)}.

Write Qb​(𝜽,s)Q_{b}(\bm{\theta};s) for the model produced by the simplified GPTQ model at precision bb and scale ss, whose channel operations are specified below. We evaluate each averaging kernel using the expected reconstruction error

ℰb​(𝒘):=12​𝔼​[‖Qb​(𝜽T𝒘,s⁡(𝒘))−𝝁T‖𝑮2].\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}):=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\|Q_{b}(\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}};s(\bm{w}))-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}\right]. (53)

This sums the squared channel-output differences between the quantized averaged model and the latest latent mean. It includes the temporal lag and spatial noise already present before quantization, together with the change caused by quantization. We assume that every channel matrix 𝑮(ℓ,i)\bm{G}^{(\ell,i)} is positive definite.

The simplified GPTQ model quantizes one group of coordinates and uses the other to compensate for its output error. Partition each channel into two nonempty groups f\mathrm{f} and r\mathrm{r}. Reorder the stacked coordinates so that all f\mathrm{f} entries precede all r\mathrm{r} entries, and apply the same permutation to every global vector and matrix. We retain the symbols 𝜽\bm{\theta} and 𝑮\bm{G} in this order. Then

𝜽=(𝜽f𝜽r),𝑮=(𝑮f,f𝑮f,r𝑮r,f𝑮r,r).\bm{\theta}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}\\ \bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{r}}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\bm{G}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{f}}&\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{r}}\\ \bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{f}}&\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\end{pmatrix}.

To simplify the theoretical analysis, we do not model group-wise quantization scales. Instead, we assign the averaged state a single scale, computed before rounding from its RMS magnitude.

Assumption A.4 (Fixed RMS Scale).

For each averaging kernel 𝒘\bm{w}, the scale is

s​(𝒘)2:=1P​𝔼​‖𝜽T𝒘‖22=‖𝝁T𝒘‖22P+σ2​R​(𝒘).s(\bm{w})^{2}:=\frac{1}{P}\mathbb{E}\|\bm{\theta}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{\|\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}}\|_{2}^{2}}{P}+\sigma^{2}R(\bm{w}).

Δb,g​(𝒘):=2​Hg​s​(𝒘)2b−1,Δ¯b,g:=Δb,g​(𝒘)s⁡(𝒘)=2​Hg2b−1.\Delta_{b,\mathrm{g}}(\bm{w}):=\frac{2H_{\mathrm{g}}s(\bm{w})}{2^{b}-1},\qquad\bar{\Delta}_{b,\mathrm{g}}:=\frac{\Delta_{b,\mathrm{g}}(\bm{w})}{s(\bm{w})}=\frac{2H_{\mathrm{g}}}{2^{b}-1}.

[−Hg​s​(𝒘),Hg​s​(𝒘)].[-H_{\mathrm{g}}s(\bm{w}),\,H_{\mathrm{g}}s(\bm{w})].

Deterministic rounding generally leads to less tractable rounding-error statistics (Alvarez et al., 2025; Zhang and Saab, 2026). To simplify the analysis, following Wannamaker et al. (2000), we instead use nonsubtractive triangular dither and define

round(t):=⌊t+U+V+12⌋,U,V∼i.i.d.Unif[−1/2,1/2].\operatorname{round}(t):=\left\lfloor t+U+V+\frac{1}{2}\right\rfloor,\qquad U,V\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\operatorname{Unif}[-1/2,1/2].

Here Unif⁡[a,b]\operatorname{Unif}[a,b] denotes the uniform distribution on [a,b][a,b], and ⌊⋅⌋\lfloor\cdot\rfloor denotes the floor operator, so round⁡(t)\operatorname{round}(t) returns an integer code.

kj=clip[0,2b−1]⁡(round⁡(zjΔ+2b−12)),[quantb⁡(𝒛,s,Hg)]j=Δ⁡(kj−2b−12).k_{j}=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,2^{b}-1]}\left(\operatorname{round}\left(\frac{z_{j}}{\Delta}+\frac{2^{b}-1}{2}\right)\right),\qquad[\operatorname{quant}_{b}(\bm{z};s,H_{\mathrm{g}})]_{j}=\Delta\left(k_{j}-\frac{2^{b}-1}{2}\right).

We next derive the parameter error induced by the simplified GPTQ procedure and its corresponding output reconstruction error.

𝑪f:=𝑮f,f−𝑮f,r​𝑲.\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}:=\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{f}}-\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{r}}\bm{K}.
Lemma A.7 (Parameter and Reconstruction Errors of the Simplified GPTQ Model).

The Schur complement 𝐂f\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}} is positive definite. The quantization-induced global parameter error is

𝜹b​(𝜽,s):=Qb​(𝜽,s)−𝜽=(𝒆f−𝑲​𝒆f+𝜼r).\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s):=Q_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)-\bm{\theta}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\\ -\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}\end{pmatrix}.

Its output reconstruction error satisfies

𝜹b​(𝜽,s)⊤​𝑮​𝜹b​(𝜽,s)=𝒆f⊤​𝑪f​𝒆f+𝜼r⊤​𝑮r,r​𝜼r.\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)=\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}. (56)
Proof.

Because 𝑮≻0\bm{G}\succ 0, its principal block 𝑮r,r\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}} is positive definite. Let JJ be the global reconstruction objective in Eq. (54). For a fixed first-group error, expanding and differentiating it gives

J⁡(𝒄r)\displaystyle J(\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}) =𝒆f⊤​𝑮f,f​𝒆f+2​𝒄r⊤​𝑮r,f​𝒆f+𝒄r⊤​𝑮r,r​𝒄r,\displaystyle=\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+2\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}},
∇𝒄rJ\displaystyle\nabla_{\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}}J =2​𝑮r,f​𝒆f+2​𝑮r,r​𝒄r.\displaystyle=2\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+2\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}.

Setting this derivative to zero recovers 𝒄r⋆=−𝑲​𝒆f\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\star}=-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}.

Completing the square decomposes the reconstruction error into the residual error after optimal compensation and the additional error from a non-optimal compensation:

J⁡(𝒄r)=𝒆f⊤​𝑪f​𝒆f⏟residual error+(𝒄r+𝑲​𝒆f)⊤​𝑮r,r​(𝒄r+𝑲​𝒆f)⏟compensation error.J(\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}})=\underbrace{\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}}_{\text{residual error}}+\underbrace{(\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}+\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}})^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}(\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}+\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}})}_{\text{compensation error}}. (57)

This identity holds for every first-group rounding error 𝒆f\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}. At the optimum, 𝒄r⋆=−𝑲​𝒆f\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\star}=-\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}, so the second term in Eq. (57) vanishes and

𝒆f⊤​𝑪f​𝒆f=(𝒆f−𝑲​𝒆f)⊤​𝑮​(𝒆f−𝑲​𝒆f)>0(𝒆f≠𝟎).\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\\ -\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top}\bm{G}\begin{pmatrix}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\\ -\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\end{pmatrix}>0\qquad(\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}\neq\bm{0}).

Hence 𝑪f≻0\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\succ 0. The second rounding introduces the additional error 𝜼r\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}, so that

𝒄r=𝒄r⋆+𝜼r,\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}=\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\star}+\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}},

therefore

𝒄r+𝑲​𝒆f=𝜼r,\bm{c}_{\mathrm{r}}+\bm{K}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}=\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}},

Substituting this expression into Eq. (57) gives

J=𝒆f⊤​𝑪f​𝒆f+𝜼r⊤​𝑮r,r​𝜼r,J=\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}},

which proves Eq. (56). ∎

Lemma A.7 gives the parameter and reconstruction errors of the simplified GPTQ model. We use this result to analyze the quantization-induced contribution to ℰb​(𝒘)\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}). Let

𝒂:=𝜽−𝝁T=(𝒂f𝒂r).\bm{a}:=\bm{\theta}-\bm{\mu}_{T}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{a}_{\mathrm{f}}\\ \bm{a}_{\mathrm{r}}\end{pmatrix}.

we have

Qb​(𝜽,s)−𝝁T=𝒂+𝜹b​(𝜽,s),Q_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)-\bm{\mu}_{T}=\bm{a}+\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s),

and the change in reconstruction error introduced by quantization is

12​‖𝒂+𝜹b​(𝜽,s)‖𝑮2−12​‖𝒂‖𝑮2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\bm{a}+\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)\right\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{a}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2} (58)
=𝒂f⊤​𝑪f​𝒆f+𝒂f⊤​𝑮f,r​𝜼r+𝒂r⊤​𝑮r,r​𝜼r+12​𝒆f⊤​𝑪f​𝒆f+12​𝜼r⊤​𝑮r,r​𝜼r.\displaystyle=\bm{a}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\bm{a}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{f},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}+\bm{a}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}+\frac{1}{2}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{e}_{\mathrm{f}}+\frac{1}{2}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}\bm{G}_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{r}}\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}}.

Eq. (58) separates the quantization-induced change into linear and quadratic rounding terms. We first fix the input and take the expectation over the rounding randomness, then take the expectation over the spatial noise. The resulting moments give the exact expected contribution of each term. Partition 𝝁T=(𝝁T,f⊤,𝝁T,r⊤)⊤\bm{\mu}_{T}=(\bm{\mu}_{T,\mathrm{f}}^{\top},\bm{\mu}_{T,\mathrm{r}}^{\top})^{\top} in the same way as 𝜽\bm{\theta}. Substituting 𝒂=𝜽−𝝁T\bm{a}=\bm{\theta}-\bm{\mu}_{T} into Eq. (58) and expanding the quadratic forms gives

𝔼⁡[12​‖𝒂+𝜹b​(𝜽,s)‖𝑮2−12​‖𝒂‖𝑮2]=𝒯1+𝒯2+𝒯3+𝒯4,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{a}+\bm{\delta}_{b}(\bm{\theta};s)\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{a}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}\right]=\mathcal{T}_{1}+\mathcal{T}_{2}+\mathcal{T}_{3}+\mathcal{T}_{4}, (59)

Here the four terms are

The remaining terms are quadratic in the rounding errors: 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} collects coordinatewise squares, and 𝒯4\mathcal{T}_{4} collects cross-coordinate products. The following lemma gives the conditional moments needed to evaluate these terms.

For the first group, condition on the full input 𝜽\bm{\theta}. Eq. (62) connects the expected reconstruction error to the lag-induced displacement of the averaged mean and the retained spatial noise. To make this dependence explicit along the LNWA frontier, we use mean age to parameterize temporal lag, derive the corresponding retained noise factor, and track the averaged latent mean. These relations determine the transition from tolerance to degradation.

Recall that the LNWA frontier is the family 𝒘λ\bm{w}_{\lambda}. The LAWA kernel 𝒘LAWA\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{LAWA}}} has mean age m0:=m⁡(𝒘LAWA)=(M−1)/2m_{0}:=m(\bm{w}^{\textnormal{{LAWA}}})=(M-1)/2. We measure the reduction from LAWA by

y:=m0−m⁡(𝒘λ),0≤y≤m0.y:=m_{0}-m(\bm{w}_{\lambda}),\qquad 0\leq y\leq m_{0}.

Thus y=0y=0 corresponds to LAWA, while y=m0y=m_{0} corresponds to the most recent saved weight. The frontier coordinates in Lemma A.5 show that mean age decreases strictly as λ\lambda increases. Hence each y<m0y<m_{0} determines a unique λ⁡(y)\lambda(y). To simplify notation, we write 𝒘⁡(y):=𝒘λ⁡(y)\bm{w}(y):=\bm{w}_{\lambda(y)} for that kernel. We also write m⁡(y):=m⁡(𝒘⁡(y))=m0−ym(y):=m(\bm{w}(y))=m_{0}-y and R⁡(y):=R⁡(𝒘⁡(y))R(y):=R(\bm{w}(y)) for its mean age and retained noise factor. For notational consistency, primes below denote derivatives along this parameterized frontier. In particular,

ℰb′​(y):=dd​y​ℰb​(𝒘⁡(y)),ℰb′′​(y):=d2d​y2​ℰb​(𝒘⁡(y)),\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(y):=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(y)),\qquad\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime\prime}(y):=\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}y^{2}}\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(y)),

and analogously for 𝒫0\mathcal{P}_{0} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. After the later change of variable to xx, primes correspondingly denote derivatives with respect to xx. Thus mean weight age decreases linearly with yy; the accompanying change in spatial noise is determined next from the frontier kernel.

On a segment with q≥2q\geq 2 active saved weights, the positive coefficients have ages 0,…,q−10,\ldots,q-1. Uniform averaging over these weights has mean age d¯q=(q−1)/2\bar{d}_{q}=(q-1)/2. The reduction relative to this local baseline is

zq:=d¯q−m⁡(y)=y−M−q2.z_{q}:=\bar{d}_{q}-m(y)=y-\frac{M-q}{2}.

Lemma A.5 then gives the kernel coefficients

wd​(y)={1q+zq​(d¯q−d)Dq,0≤d<q,0,d≥q,w_{d}(y)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{q}+\frac{z_{q}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)}{D_{q}},&0\leq d<q,\\[4.0pt] 0,&d\geq q,\end{cases} (63)

where Dq:=q⁡(q2−1)/12D_{q}:=q(q^{2}-1)/12. Squaring and summing the coefficients therefore gives the spatial noise factor

R⁡(y)=∑d=0q−1wd​(y)2=1q+zq2Dq,R(y)=\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}w_{d}(y)^{2}=\frac{1}{q}+\frac{z_{q}^{2}}{D_{q}},

whose derivatives are

R′​(y)=2​zqDq,R′′​(y)=2Dq.R^{\prime}(y)=\frac{2z_{q}}{D_{q}},\qquad R^{\prime\prime}(y)=\frac{2}{D_{q}}.

Finally, the original frontier parameter is recovered from zq=Dq​λ​m​(y)z_{q}=D_{q}\lambda m(y) as

λ⁡(y)=zqDq​(m0−y).\lambda(y)=\frac{z_{q}}{D_{q}(m_{0}-y)}. (64)

The endpoint is y=m0y=m_{0}, with λ⁡(m0)=∞\lambda(m_{0})=\infty. Write 𝝁⁡(y):=𝝁T𝒘⁡(y)\bm{\mu}(y):=\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}(y)} for the latent mean of this averaged state. It is affine within each support segment because the averaging coefficients are affine there. Using the latent-mean increments defined in Appendix A.1, its derivative is

𝒂q:=𝝁′​(y)\displaystyle\bm{a}_{q}:=\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y) =1Dq​∑d=0q−1(d¯q−d)​𝝁T−d\displaystyle=\frac{1}{D_{q}}\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)\bm{\mu}_{T-d}
=1Dq​∑d=0q−1(d¯q−d)​(𝝁T−q+1+∑j=d+1q−1𝒗T−j+1)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{D_{q}}\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)\left(\bm{\mu}_{T-q+1}+\sum_{j=d+1}^{q-1}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\right)
=1Dq​∑j=1q−1(∑d=0j−1(d¯q−d))​𝒗T−j+1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{D_{q}}\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\left(\sum_{d=0}^{j-1}(\bar{d}_{q}-d)\right)\bm{v}_{T-j+1}

∑j=1q−1j⁡(q−j)2​Dq=1.\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\frac{j(q-j)}{2D_{q}}=1.

Thus 𝒂q\bm{a}_{q} is a convex combination of the retained mean increments; its norm is at most v¯:=max1≤j<M⁡‖𝒗T−j+1‖2\bar{v}:=\max_{1\leq j<M}\|\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\|_{2}. We use this increment bound below to control changes in the averaged mean at support boundaries.

On a fixed-support segment, 𝝁′​(y)=𝒂q\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y)=\bm{a}_{q} is constant and R′′​(y)=2/DqR^{\prime\prime}(y)=2/D_{q}. The two components have second derivatives

Consequently,

ℰb′′​(y)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime\prime}(y) =𝒫0′′​(y)+γb​𝒬′′​(y)\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime\prime}(y)+\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime}(y) (65)
=𝒂q⊤​𝑮​𝒂q+2​γb​‖𝒂q‖22+2​NG+2​γb​P​σ2Dq>0.\displaystyle=\bm{a}_{q}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{a}_{q}+2\gamma_{b}\|\bm{a}_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{2N_{G}+2\gamma_{b}P\sigma^{2}}{D_{q}}>0.

These results describe movement within one support segment. When the oldest positive averaging coefficient reaches zero, the active set changes and 𝝁′​(y)\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(y) can jump. We next relate these changes to the evolution of the latent mean over the retained window.

Across nearby saved weights in a stable training phase, latent-mean increments are small and change gradually with normalized training time. The following regularity condition bounds their magnitudes and adjacent variation.

Assumption A.6 (Local Regularity of the Latent Mean).

Measure training time as t/Tt/T. The MM consecutive retained weights span the normalized length ℓ:=(M−1)/T\ell:=(M-1)/T, with spacing h:=1/T=ℓ/(M−1)h:=1/T=\ell/(M-1). The forward latent increments satisfy

‖𝒗T−j+1‖2≤V​h(1≤j<M),‖𝒗T−j+1−𝒗T−j+2‖2≤A​h2(2≤j<M),\|\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\|_{2}\leq Vh\quad(1\leq j<M),\qquad\|\bm{v}_{T-j+1}-\bm{v}_{T-j+2}\|_{2}\leq Ah^{2}\quad(2\leq j<M),

where V,A≥0V,A\geq 0 are uniform over the considered late-training windows and independent of the spacing hh.

Summing the dd increments between 𝝁T−d\bm{\mu}_{T-d} and 𝝁T\bm{\mu}_{T} gives

‖𝝁T−d−𝝁T‖2≤V​d​h.\|\bm{\mu}_{T-d}-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{2}\leq Vdh.

Theorem A.2 (Finite Noise Tolerance and Degradation).

Under Assumptions A.3–A.7, for sufficiently large TT, consider the expected reconstruction error ℰb=𝒫0+γb​𝒬\mathcal{E}_{b}=\mathcal{P}_{0}+\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q} at a fixed precision b≥bminb\geq b_{\min}. It is zero if ℰb′​(0+)≥0\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0+)\geq 0; otherwise, it is the unique positive solution of ℰb​(τb)=ℰb​(0)\mathcal{E}_{b}(\tau_{b})=\mathcal{E}_{b}(0). Proof.

Recall that Fb​(y)F_{b}(y) is the error change from 𝒘⁡(0)\bm{w}(0) divided by yy, with Fb​(0)F_{b}(0) equal to the initial right slope in yy. Since y=m0​xy=m_{0}x, ℰb′​(0+)=m0​Fb​(0)\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0+)=m_{0}F_{b}(0), so the two initial slopes have the same sign.

A.6 Precision-dependent averaging preference

The first main theorem compares the expected reconstruction error ℰb\mathcal{E}_{b} with its value at LAWA for a fixed precision. We now determine how quantization precision shifts the preferred kernel and identify the precision at which its lag–noise preference changes.

Recall that x=1−m/m0x=1-m/m_{0} increases from uniform averaging toward the most recent saved weight. Increasing xx reduces mean weight age and retains more spatial noise. Write 𝝁⁡(x)=𝝁T𝒘⁡(m0​x)\bm{\mu}(x)=\bm{\mu}_{T}^{\bm{w}(m_{0}x)} and R⁡(x)=R⁡(𝒘⁡(m0​x))R(x)=R(\bm{w}(m_{0}x)). For any frontier function in this subsection, an argument xx means evaluation at 𝒘⁡(m0​x)\bm{w}(m_{0}x); in particular, ℰb​(x)=ℰb​(𝒘⁡(m0​x))\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)=\mathcal{E}_{b}(\bm{w}(m_{0}x)). The exact identity in Lemma A.9 separates the unquantized error and the quantization contribution:

ℰb​(x)=𝒫0​(x)+γb​𝒬​(x),\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)=\mathcal{P}_{0}(x)+\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q}(x),

where γb:=cG/(2b−1)2\gamma_{b}:=c_{G}/(2^{b}-1)^{2}. Its two precision-independent components are

𝒫0​(x)=12​‖𝝁⁡(x)−𝝁T‖𝑮2+NG​R​(x),𝒬⁡(x)=‖𝝁⁡(x)‖22+P​σ2​R​(x).\mathcal{P}_{0}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}(x)-\bm{\mu}_{T}\|_{\bm{G}}^{2}+N_{G}R(x),\qquad\mathcal{Q}(x)=\|\bm{\mu}(x)\|_{2}^{2}+P\sigma^{2}R(x).

Here 𝒫0\mathcal{P}_{0} is the unquantized reconstruction error, and γb​𝒬\gamma_{b}\mathcal{Q} is the quantization contribution under the simplified GPTQ model. The coefficients NGN_{G} and cG>0c_{G}>0 were defined in the preceding subsection. Precision enters ℰb\mathcal{E}_{b} through γb\gamma_{b}, which increases as precision decreases. The effect of this increase depends on how 𝒬\mathcal{Q} varies with xx.

We assume that, during a stable training phase, latent-mean increments are aligned with one another and with the latent mean at the start of the retained window.

Assumption A.8 (Pairwise Alignment of Latent-Mean Increments).

The latent increments in the retained window satisfy

𝒗T−i+1⊤​𝒗T−j+1≥0(1≤i,j<M).\bm{v}_{T-i+1}^{\top}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\geq 0\qquad(1\leq i,j<M).
Assumption A.9 (Alignment with the Oldest Retained Latent Mean).

The latent increments also satisfy

𝝁T−M+1⊤​𝒗T−j+1≥0(1≤j<M).\bm{\mu}_{T-M+1}^{\top}\bm{v}_{T-j+1}\geq 0\qquad(1\leq j<M).

Assumption A.8 says that the progress increments do not oppose one another; Assumption A.9 says that they do not oppose the oldest retained latent mean. Their magnitudes and directions may differ. The next lemma uses both sets of inner products to show that favoring more recent saved weights cannot decrease the latent-mean norm.

𝝁​(x)⊤​𝝁′​(x)≥0.\bm{\mu}(x)^{\top}\bm{\mu}^{\prime}(x)\geq 0.
