Beyond the first segment, both 𝒫0′\mathcal{P}_{0}^{\prime} and 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} are positive. Hence this zero is the unique global minimizer of ℰb\mathcal{E}_{b}. ∎

Lemma A.14 gives the global minimizer at each evaluated precision. In Eq. (78), precision enters only through γb\gamma_{b}: lower precision increases this coefficient and gives more weight to the quantization cost, while higher precision reduces it. This changes the optimal trade-off between denoising and reducing temporal lag. The following theorem identifies the precision at which that preference changes and proves how the optimum responds.

Theorem A.3 (Precision-Dependent Averaging Preference).

Under Assumptions A.3–A.10, for sufficiently large TT, define

bcrit:=log2⁡(1+2​cG​𝝁¯⊤​𝒖𝒖⊤​𝑮​(𝝁T−𝝁¯)).b_{\mathrm{crit}}:=\log_{2}\!\left(1+\sqrt{\frac{2c_{G}\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}}{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})}}\right). (79)

For every evaluated precision b≥bminb\geq b_{\min},

b≤bcrit\displaystyle b\leq b_{\mathrm{crit}} ⟹xb=0,τb=0(less spatial noise),\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad x_{b}=0,\quad\tau_{b}=0\qquad\text{{(less spatial noise)}},
b>bcrit\displaystyle b>b_{\mathrm{crit}} ⟹xb>0,τb>0(less temporal lag).\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad x_{b}>0,\quad\tau_{b}>0\qquad\text{{(less temporal lag)}}.

The optimal position xbx_{b} is nondecreasing in bb and strictly increasing in the regime b>bcritb>b_{\mathrm{crit}}. If bcrit<bminb_{\mathrm{crit}}<b_{\min}, all evaluated precisions lie in the second regime.

Proof.

By Lemma A.14, xbx_{b} is determined by the sign of ℰb′​(0+)\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0^{+}). Since

ℰb′​(0+)=𝒖⊤​𝑮​(𝝁¯−𝝁T)+2​cG​𝝁¯⊤​𝒖(2b−1)2,\mathcal{E}_{b}^{\prime}(0^{+})=\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bar{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu}_{T})+\frac{2c_{G}\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}}{(2^{b}-1)^{2}},

this slope is nonnegative exactly when b≤bcritb\leq b_{\mathrm{crit}}. The equivalence also holds when 𝝁¯⊤​𝒖=0\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}=0, in which case bcrit=0b_{\mathrm{crit}}=0 and every evaluated precision has a negative initial slope. Theorem A.2 then gives τb=0\tau_{b}=0 in the nonnegative-slope regime and τb>0\tau_{b}>0 in the negative-slope regime.

Where the maximum in Eq. (78) is positive, differentiation with respect to γb\gamma_{b} gives

dd​γb​(𝒖⊤​𝑮​(𝝁T−𝝁¯)−2​γb​𝝁¯⊤​𝒖a+c​γb)=−2​a​𝝁¯⊤​𝒖+c​𝒖⊤​𝑮​(𝝁T−𝝁¯)(a+c​γb)2<0.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\gamma_{b}}\left(\frac{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})-2\gamma_{b}\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}}{a+c\gamma_{b}}\right)=-\frac{2a\bar{\bm{\mu}}^{\top}\bm{u}+c\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{\mu}_{T}-\bar{\bm{\mu}})}{(a+c\gamma_{b})^{2}}<0.

As γb\gamma_{b} strictly decreases with bb, xbx_{b} is nondecreasing overall and strictly increasing above the threshold. ∎

Together, these results characterize the optimal kernel’s shift in lag–noise preference: lower precision favors denoising, whereas higher precision favors reducing temporal lag. Eq. (79) gives the explicit precision threshold for this transition.

Appendix B Key Assumptions and Limitation

B.1 Empirical Assessment of Key Assumptions

Our assumptions concern the latent mean, which is defined as a conditional expectation over training randomness. The law of large numbers gives, at each fixed training step tt,

𝝁^t(n):=1n​∑r=1n𝜽t(r)→n→∞a.s.𝔼⁡[𝜽t∣ℱ0]=𝝁t.\widehat{\bm{\mu}}_{t}^{(n)}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\bm{\theta}_{t}^{(r)}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\mathrm{a.s.}}\mathbb{E}[\bm{\theta}_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{0}]=\bm{\mu}_{t}.

Repeated runs let us estimate the latent mean and spatial noise. Since rerunning LLM pretraining many times is costly, we use a small neural network to compare trajectories across runs and empirically assess our key assumptions.

Experimental setup.

We train a two-layer ReLU multilayer perceptron (MLP) on MNIST dataset. Images are average-pooled to 14×1414\times 14 and standardized, and the network has dimensions 196→64→10196\to 64\to 10. We train the full network with SGD and analyze its 650 output-layer weights and biases, denoted by 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t}. To reflect the single-epoch data consumption of LLM pretraining, we sample without replacement throughout training. We split MNIST into 58,000 training and 2,000 validation images, train a shared prefix on 16,000 images, and then branch into 16 runs that traverse the remaining data in different orders. Across the 16 branches, we estimate the latent mean and spatial noise by

𝝁^t(16)=116​∑r=116𝜽t(r),ϵ^t(r)=𝜽t(r)−𝝁^t(16).\widehat{\bm{\mu}}_{t}^{(16)}=\frac{1}{16}\sum_{r=1}^{16}\bm{\theta}_{t}^{(r)},\qquad\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t}^{(r)}=\bm{\theta}_{t}^{(r)}-\widehat{\bm{\mu}}_{t}^{(16)}.

The shared prefix uses 500 updates at batch size 32 and learning rate 0.030.03. Each branch then runs for 1,000 updates. We vary the continuation learning rate over {0.01,0.02,0.03}\{0.01,0.02,0.03\} at batch size 32 and the batch size over {24,32,40}\{24,32,40\} at learning rate 0.030.03.

Spatial noise decorrelation.

Figure 6 measures the correlation between spatial noise at different training positions. Let 𝒯:={500,…,1000}\mathcal{T}:=\{500,\ldots,1000\} denote the updates in the analysis window. For a saving interval hh, let 𝒯h:={t∈𝒯:t−h≥0}\mathcal{T}_{h}:=\{t\in\mathcal{T}:t-h\geq 0\} denote the endpoints for which both ϵ^t−h\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t-h} and ϵ^t\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t} are available. We evaluate the correlation as

ρ^ϵ​(h):=∑t∈𝒯h∑r=116⟨ϵ^t−h(r),ϵ^t(r)⟩∑t∈𝒯h∑r=116‖ϵ^t−h(r)‖22​∑t∈𝒯h∑r=116‖ϵ^t(r)‖22,\widehat{\rho}_{\epsilon}(h):=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{h}}\sum_{r=1}^{16}\bigl\langle\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t-h}^{(r)},\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t}^{(r)}\bigr\rangle}{\displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{h}}\sum_{r=1}^{16}\|\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t-h}^{(r)}\|_{2}^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{h}}\sum_{r=1}^{16}\|\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t}^{(r)}\|_{2}^{2}}},

The correlation decreases steadily with hh. At h=500h=500, it is 0.1010.101–0.1170.117 across learning rates and decreases from 0.1680.168 to 0.0150.015 as the batch size increases from 24 to 40. This supports the weak temporal dependence used in Assumption A.1 for sparsely saved weights.

Spatial noise dispersion.

Figure 7 uses eight branches to identify the principal directions of spatial noise and the remaining eight to evaluate them. Let ℛfit\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{fit}} and ℛeval\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{eval}} denote these two sets. We recompute the latent-mean estimate within each set and obtain the corresponding residuals ϵ^t,fit(r)\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t,\mathrm{fit}}^{(r)} and ϵ^t,eval(r)\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t,\mathrm{eval}}^{(r)}. From the fitting set, we form the empirical noise covariance

𝚺^fit:=1|𝒯|​|ℛfit|​∑t∈𝒯∑r∈ℛfitϵ^t,fit(r)​(ϵ^t,fit(r))⊤.\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathrm{fit}}:=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|\,|\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{fit}}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{fit}}}\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t,\mathrm{fit}}^{(r)}\bigl(\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t,\mathrm{fit}}^{(r)}\bigr)^{\top}.

Let 𝑼k∈ℝ650×k\bm{U}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{650\times k} contain the orthonormal eigenvectors associated with its kk largest eigenvalues. We then measure how much spatial-noise variance these directions capture on the evaluation branches:

V^ϵ​(k):=100×∑t∈𝒯∑r∈ℛeval‖𝑼k⊤​ϵ^t,eval(r)‖22∑t∈𝒯∑r∈ℛeval‖ϵ^t,eval(r)‖22%.\widehat{V}_{\epsilon}(k):=100\times\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{eval}}}\|\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t,\mathrm{eval}}^{(r)}\|_{2}^{2}}{\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{eval}}}\|\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t,\mathrm{eval}}^{(r)}\|_{2}^{2}}\,\%.

The parameter space has 650 dimensions. If the noise were concentrated in only a few directions, the first ten directions would explain a large fraction of its variance; rank-one noise, for example, would be captured entirely by the first direction. Instead, the first ten directions explain only 3.98%3.98\%–6.24%6.24\% of the variance. Thus the spatial noise is not concentrated in a small number of directions but dispersed across many parameter directions. For analytical simplicity, Assumption A.3 models this dispersed spatial noise with an isotropic covariance.

Alignment between progress increments.

Let t0<⋯<t9t_{0}<\cdots<t_{9} be the ten selected positions and define the run-specific increments Δ​𝜽j(r):=𝜽tj(r)−𝜽tj−1(r)\Delta\bm{\theta}_{j}^{(r)}:=\bm{\theta}_{t_{j}}^{(r)}-\bm{\theta}_{t_{j-1}}^{(r)}. Figure 8 estimates the inner product between latent-mean increments using distinct runs,

A^i​j:=116⋅15​∑r≠s⟨Δ​𝜽i(r),Δ​𝜽j(s)⟩,1≤i<j≤9.\widehat{A}_{ij}:=\frac{1}{16\cdot 15}\sum_{r\neq s}\bigl\langle\Delta\bm{\theta}_{i}^{(r)},\Delta\bm{\theta}_{j}^{(s)}\bigr\rangle,\qquad 1\leq i<j\leq 9.

Each increment is first computed within one branch. In A^i​j\widehat{A}_{ij}, the increment at position ii from branch rr is paired with the increment at position jj from a different branch s≠rs\neq r, and the result is averaged over all 16⋅1516\cdot 15 ordered branch pairs. Because the two branches have independent zero-mean fluctuations, their noise terms vanish in expectation. Hence A^i​j\widehat{A}_{ij} estimates the inner product between the corresponding latent-mean increments. All 36 pairs are positive in every setting, showing that recent progress tends to remain aligned and supporting Assumption A.8.

Alignment with the window-start mean.

Figure 9 measures the inner products between the latent mean at the start of the analysis window and the nine subsequent progress increments. It uses the similar cross-run estimate

B^j:=116⋅15​∑r≠s⟨𝜽t0(r),Δ​𝜽j(s)⟩,1≤j≤9.\widehat{B}_{j}:=\frac{1}{16\cdot 15}\sum_{r\neq s}\bigl\langle\bm{\theta}_{t_{0}}^{(r)},\Delta\bm{\theta}_{j}^{(s)}\bigr\rangle,\qquad 1\leq j\leq 9.

All nine values are positive in every setting, supporting Assumption A.9.

B.2 Limitation

The main limitation of our work is that the theoretical guarantees are established under an idealized setting. However, bridging tractable theory and practical quantization pipelines is a broader challenge for the community rather than our uniqueness. In particular, our training analysis makes assumptions about the latent mean and spatial noise. We provide an empirical assessment of the key assumptions in Section B.1, which offers support for the theoretical setting. Our quantization analysis adopts a simplified GPTQ model: we use randomized dither rounding rather than deterministic nearest rounding, which has well-established statistical properties and has been used in quantization theory (Wannamaker et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2023; Dirksen et al., 2025); we also use a global scale rather than group-wise scales and consider only a two-stage quantization and compensation process. Such simplifications are common and widely accepted in the community (Banner et al., 2018; Nagel et al., 2020; Chee et al., 2023). Future work will further develop the theory toward more practical quantization settings.

Appendix C Additional Experimental Results

C.1 Experimental Settings

Pretraining settings.

We pretrain OPT-series models (Zhang et al., 2022) (125M, 350M, and 1.3B) from scratch on FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024), with the model-specific configurations summarized in Table 2. Each training example is a sequence of length 512, and the global batch size denotes the number of such sequences processed per optimizer update. We use AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017) with (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.95)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) and ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8} throughout training. The LR is linearly warmed up to its peak value during the first 1%1\% of training and kept constant for the following 89%89\%. Over the final 10%10\%, we either continue training at the peak LR or transition to a cosine decay schedule, yielding the stable-LR and LR decay baselines, respectively. For weight averaging, we save the last M=10M=10 weights from each stable-LR trajectory at intervals of 500 optimizer steps (Catalan-Tatjer et al., 2026). All experiments are run on 4 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs.

Post-training quantization settings.

For both GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024), we use the same calibration set, consisting of 128 length-512 sequences deterministically sampled from a fixed English C4 training split (Raffel et al., 2020). Both methods use a group size of 128 and are evaluated at 4-bit (W4), 3-bit (W3), and 2-bit (W2) precision. For GPTQ, we use 1%1\% Hessian damping, disable activation ordering, and set the column block size to 128. For AWQ, we use asymmetric affine quantization with zero points, with scaling exponent α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and clipping ratio c=0.8c=0.8. We evaluate every quantized endpoint on 1,024 blocks from a fixed held-out RefinedWeb split. All remaining quantization settings are kept identical across model sizes.

Averaging kernels and coefficient grids.

The tolerance-to-degradation experiment evaluates the same coefficients λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] at every model size and precision. The precision-preference comparison uses LAWA, WMA, and LNWA with λ∈{0.002,0.004,0.006,0.008}\lambda\in\{0.002,0.004,0.006,0.008\}. The LNWA-equivalent coefficients of the fixed baselines are 00 for LAWA and approximately 0.0060610.006061 for WMA. Appendix A.4 derives these relations.

For each model–precision panel, we form n=6n=6 pairs (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) from LAWA, WMA, and LNWA with λ∈{0.002,0.004,0.006,0.008}\lambda\in\{0.002,0.004,0.006,0.008\}, where xix_{i} is the endpoint’s LNWA-equivalent coefficient and yiy_{i} is its measured PPL. The black line is the ordinary least-squares fit

(a^,b^)=arg⁡min⁡∑i=1na,b⁡[yi−(a+b​xi)]2,(\hat{a},\hat{b})=\arg\min_{a,b}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl[y_{i}-(a+bx_{i})\bigr]^{2},

and each panel reports the Pearson correlation

r=∑i=1n(xi−x¯)​(yi−y¯)∑i=1n(xi−x¯)2​∑i=1n(yi−y¯)2∈[−1,1].r=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}-\bar{x})(y_{i}-\bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}-\bar{x})^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}-\bar{y})^{2}}}\in[-1,1].

Here x¯\bar{x} and y¯\bar{y} are the sample means of the nn coefficient and PPL values, respectively. Lower PPL indicates better performance. A negative correlation associates larger λ\lambda, and hence less lag, with lower PPL. A positive correlation associates smaller λ\lambda, and hence less noise, with lower PPL. The magnitude |r||r| measures the strength of the linear association across the six endpoints.

C.2 Experimental Results

From noise tolerance to degradation.

Figures 10 and 11 extend Figure 3 to OPT-125M, OPT-350M, and OPT-1.3B, including full precision (FP) and 4-bit (W4), 3-bit (W3), and 2-bit (W2) quantization under GPTQ and AWQ, respectively. FP is evaluated on the original FineWeb-Edu validation set, whereas W4/W3/W2 are evaluated on the fixed held-out RefinedWeb validation set.

At small λ\lambda, NLL remains close to or below the LAWA baseline; at larger λ\lambda, it rises above the baseline. Reducing temporal lag can initially offset or outweigh the cost of retaining additional spatial noise. Further movement along the frontier retains more noise and degrades performance. These results across model scales and quantization methods further support the tolerance-to-degradation transition predicted by Theorem 4.2.

Precision changes the preferred averaging kernel.

Figures 12 and 13 extend Figure 4 to OPT-125M, OPT-350M, and OPT-1.3B, including FP, W4, W3, and W2, with GPTQ and AWQ, respectively. At every model scale, PPL is positively correlated with the averaging coefficient at W2 and negatively correlated at W4 under both methods. Since smaller coefficients retain less spatial noise and larger coefficients reduce temporal lag, the reversal indicates a preference for less noise at lower precision and less lag at higher precision. This further supports the precision-dependent preference predicted by Theorem 4.3.

Comparison with learning-rate decay.

We compare continued stable-learning-rate training, cosine decay to zero, cosine decay to 1%1\% of the maximum learning rate, and LNWA on OPT-125M. Validation loss and perplexity are recorded every 200 optimizer steps, including the shared starting weight and the final weights. The LNWA endpoint uses λ=0.008\lambda=0.008 and is shown at the final step.

Figure 14 shows that LNWA reaches a validation PPL of 31.79, compared with 35.58 for continued stable-LR training and 31.31 and 31.38 for decay to 1%1\% LR and zero, respectively.

Figure 15 shows that the final Hessian trace is 1,385 for LNWA, compared with 1,605 for stable LR and 1,835 and 1,859 for the two decay schedules. Weight averaging therefore achieves validation performance close to LR decay while maintaining lower local curvature.
